title: Remembering Pionius to strengthen imitators
english: The Apostle urges us to take part in the remembrances of the saints, knowing that remembering those who finished their course soundly, with their whole heart, in faith, steadies all who desire to imitate what is better.

Of the martyr Pionius we ought to keep remembrance all the more, for both while he sojourned in the world he turned many from wandering as an apostolic man in our own day, and at the last, when he was called to the Lord and bore his martyrdom, he left this account behind for our instruction, so that even now we possess memorials of his teaching.

title: Arrest on Polycarp's anniversary
english: In the sixth month, on the second day as the great Sabbath was coming on, on the anniversary of the blessed martyr Polycarp, while the persecution under Decius was still upon them, Pionius the presbyter and Sabina the confessor and Asclepiades and Macedonia and Linus, a presbyter of the catholic church, were arrested. Pionius had seen one day before the anniversary of Polycarp that they were to be seized on that very day. He was then keeping a fast with Sabina and Asclepiades, and because he had seen that they were to be seized on the morrow, he took three chains and set them about his own neck and the neck of Sabina and of Asclepiades, and they waited in the house. He did this for those who would come to take him, lest anyone should suspect that they were going aside like the rest to eat defiled food, but that all might know they had resolved to be carried off straight to prison.

title: Seized on the Sabbath and brought to the market
english: After they had been arrested and had taken the holy bread and water on the Sabbath, Polemon the temple-warden came upon them with the men assigned with him to hunt out Christians and drag them to sacrifice and to eat food defiled by idols. The warden said, You surely know the emperor's decree, which commands you to sacrifice to the gods. Pionius answered, We know the commandments of God, in which he commands us to worship him alone. Polemon said, Come then to the marketplace, and there you will be made to comply. Sabina and Asclepiades answered, We obey the living God. So he brought them without using force.

As they walked on, all the onlookers saw that they wore chains, and as though at some marvel a crowd rushed together at speed, so that they jostled one another. When they reached the marketplace, at the eastern colonnade by the double gate, the whole marketplace and the galleries above were crowded with Greeks and Jews and women, for they were at leisure because it was a great Sabbath. People even clambered up onto the stands and onto the boxes to get a view.

title: Pionius answers Polemon before Greeks and Jews
english: So they set them in the midst, and Polemon said, Pionius, it is good for you to submit as everyone else does and to offer sacrifice, so that you will not be punished. Then Pionius stretched out his hand and answered with a bright face, saying, Men who boast in the beauty of Smyrna, who beside the Meles, as you claim, take pride in Homer, and you Jews who stand here together with them, listen while I address a few words to you. I hear that you mock and gloat over those who go over to sacrifice, and you treat their failure as sport, because they sacrifice willingly. Yet you Greeks ought to obey your own teacher Homer, who counsels that it is no holy thing to exult over the dying. And you Jews ought to heed Moses when he commands, If you see your enemy's beast fallen under its burden, you shall not pass it by but shall help raise it (Exodus 23:5). In the same way you ought to obey Solomon: If your enemy falls, he says, do not rejoice, and do not exult at his stumbling (Proverbs 24:17). If in obedience to my own Teacher I choose to die rather than break his words, and I strive not to exchange what I first learned and then also taught, at whom then are the Jews laughing without pity? For even if we are their enemies, as they say, we are still human beings, and moreover human beings who have been wronged.

They say that we enjoy seasons of bold speech. Well then, whom have we wronged? Whom have we murdered? Whom have we persecuted? Whom have we forced to worship idols? Or do they suppose that their own sins are like what is now being done by some out of human fear. But the difference is as great as the difference between willing sins and unwilling ones. For who compelled the Jews to be initiated to Baal-peor (Numbers 25:3). Or to eat the sacrifices of the dead (Psalm 106:28). Or to whore after the daughters of foreigners. Or to burn their sons and daughters to idols. Or to murmur against God. Or to speak against Moses. Or to show ingratitude while receiving benefits, or to turn back in their hearts to Egypt. Or, when Moses had gone up to receive the Law, to say to Aaron, Make us gods (Exodus 32:1), and to fashion a calf. And all the rest they did. For they are able to lead you astray. Rather, let them read to you the book of Judges, the Kingdoms, the Exodus, and all the writings in which they stand convicted. Yet they ask why some came forward on their own to sacrifice without even being compelled, and because of those men do you condemn all Christians? Do you suppose the present must be made like those ancient deeds?

title: Wheat and chaff and lands that witness to fire
english: Which heap is the greater, the heap of chaff or the heap of wheat? When the farmer comes with his winnowing fork to clean out the threshing floor, the chaff, since it is light, is easily carried away by the gust of air, but the wheat stays in the same place. Consider again the net thrown into the sea; is not everything it gathers worthless? So it is also with present things. How then do you want us to suffer these things, as unrighteous people or as righteous people? If as unrighteous, how will you yourselves escape suffering the same, since you stand convicted as unrighteous by those very deeds. But if as righteous, when the righteous suffer, what hope do you have? For if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear (1 Peter 4:18). For judgment hangs over the world, and we have been fully persuaded of it by many proofs.

For I myself traveled abroad and passed through the whole land of Judea and crossed the Jordan, and I saw a land that even to this day bears witness to the wrath of God that came upon it for the sins its dwellers committed, for they murdered strangers and drove strangers away and did violence. I saw smoke still rising from it to this day, and a land burned to ash by fire, deprived of all fruit and of all moisture. I also saw the Dead Sea, its water altered and grown feeble against nature by divine fear, unable to nourish any living creature, casting back upward by the water the one who plunges into it, and unable to keep a human body within itself. For it refuses to receive a human being, lest it be rebuked again because of a human being. These things I mention, though they are far from you. You yourselves see and speak of the fire-scorched land of Lydia of the Decapolis lying before you to this day as a warning to the ungodly, and the roaring fire of Aetna and Sicily and Lycia and the islands. And if even these are far away from you, consider the use of hot water, I mean the water that gushes up from the earth, and understand where it is kindled and where it is heated, if not as it passes through subterranean fire. Consider also partial burnings and partial floodings, such as you tell of in the days of Deucalion and we tell of in the days of Noah. Such partial events occur so that from the particular the universal may be known. Therefore we solemnly testify to you of the coming judgment through fire by God through his Word Jesus Christ. And for this reason we do not serve your so-called gods, and we do not worship the golden image.

title: The Better Life Desired
english: When these words and many others had been spoken, and Pionius had for the most part refused to fall silent, the temple-warden and his companions and the whole crowd turned their ears to listen, so that a stillness fell so deep that no one uttered even a murmur. Yet when Pionius said again, We do not serve your gods, nor do we bow down to the golden image, they led them out into the open court and placed them in the middle.

Then some men from the marketplace came and stood around them together with Polemon, pleading with him and saying, Be persuaded by us, Pionius, for we love you, and on many counts you deserve to live, for your character and your gentleness. It is good to be alive and to behold this light, with many more words besides. He answered them, I too say that life is good, but the life we long for is better. The light is good, but I mean the true light. All these present things are indeed good. We do not turn away because we condemn or hate the works of God, but because far greater things surpass them, we hold these present things in contempt, though they lie in ambush to trap us.

title: Bound for prison, not the idol shrine
english: Then a certain Alexander, a worthless fellow loitering about the marketplace, said, Hear us, Pionius. Pionius answered, Take up hearing from me, for what you know I also know, but what I understand you do not know. Alexander wanted to laugh him down, and so he said with sneering irony, But why all this? Pionius replied, All this so that as we pass through your city we may not be suspected of having come to eat defiled food, and so that you may learn that we do not even ask to be examined but have made our decision and are going not to the shrine of Nemesis but to the prison, and so that you may not seize us by violence as you did the rest and drag us off, but may let us alone because we wear chains, for with our chains upon us you will perhaps not drag us into your idol-houses. And with that Alexander was muzzled.

And again, while the others kept pleading with him at length, he kept answering, This is our decision, and he rebuked them sharply and told them of the things to come, until Alexander said, What use, he asks, are these words of yours, when you are not permitted to live?

title: Refusal to speak in the theater
english: Now the crowd wanted to hold a gathering in the theater, so that a greater number could hear him there, but some men who were anxious for the governor went to Polemon the temple-warden and said, Do not let him speak, or the people will stream into the theater and there will be an uproar and an inquiry about the man. When he heard this, Polemon said, Pionius, if you will not sacrifice, at least come to the shrine of Nemesis. He answered, But it is not good for your idols that we should come there. Polemon said, Listen to us, Pionius. Pionius said, If only I could persuade you to become Christians. At that they burst out laughing and said, There is nothing in it to make us burn alive. Pionius said, It is far worse to be burned after death.

When Sabina smiled at this, the warden and his men said, Are you laughing? She said, Yes, if God wills. For we are Christians, and all who believe in Christ without wavering shall laugh in everlasting joy. They said to her, You will suffer what you do not want, for women who refuse to sacrifice are put in a brothel. She said, The holy God will take care of that.

title: Pionius refuses to sacrifice
english: Then Polemon said to Pionius, “Let yourself be persuaded by us, Pionius.” Pionius said, “Your orders are either to persuade or to punish; since you are not persuading, punish.” Then Polemon the temple-warden put the question to him again, saying, “Offer sacrifice, Pionius.” Pionius said, “I am a Christian.” Polemon said, “What god do you worship?”

Pionius said, “God the Almighty, who made heaven and earth and all that is in them (Acts 4:24) and made all of us, who gives us all things richly (1 Timothy 6:17), whom we came to know through his Word, Christ.” Polemon said, “Then offer sacrifice at least to the emperor.” Pionius said, “I do not offer sacrifice to a human being, for I am a Christian.”

title: Questioning of the three confessors
english: Then he put the question to him for the record, with the clerk writing down everything, asking, What is your name? He answered, Pionius. Polemon said, Are you a Christian? Pionius said, Yes. Polemon the temple-warden said, Of what church? He answered, The catholic, for there is no other with Christ. Then he came to Sabina. Pionius had told her beforehand, Call yourself Theodota, so that the mere name would not put her back into the hands of the lawless Politta, who had been her mistress. For in the time of Gordian, when she wanted to draw Sabina away from the faith, Politta had her chained and sent her into exile in the mountains, where she received her provisions in secret from the brethren. Afterwards an earnest effort was made, and she was set free both from Politta and from her chains, and she lived mostly with Pionius and was arrested with him in this persecution.

So Polemon said to her as well, What is your name? She said, Theodota. He said, Are you a Christian? She said, Yes, I am a Christian. Polemon said, Of what church? Sabina said, The catholic. Polemon said, Whom do you worship? Sabina said, The almighty God who made heaven and earth and all of us, whom we have come to know through his Word, Jesus Christ. Then he questioned Asclepiades, What is your name? He said, Asclepiades. Polemon said, Are you a Christian? Asclepiades said, Yes. Polemon said, Of what church? Asclepiades said, The catholic. Polemon said, Whom do you worship? Asclepiades said, Christ Jesus. Polemon said, Is he then a different one? Asclepiades said, No, but the same one whom these have also confessed.

title: Led to prison amid mockery
english: When these things had been said, they led them away to the prison. A great crowd followed them, so that the marketplace was crowded full. Some in the crowd said about Pionius, How is it that he who is always pale now has a reddened face. As Sabina clutched hold of him by his clothing because of the shoving of the throng, some mocked them and said, Ha, like one afraid of being weaned. One man shouted aloud, If they will not offer sacrifice, let them be punished. Polemon said, But the rods do not drive us forward so that we have authority. Another said, Look, the little fellow is off to offer sacrifice.

He meant Asclepiades who was with us. Pionius said, You lie, for he is doing no such thing. Others said, Such a one and such a one have sacrificed. Pionius said, Each man has his own choice. What is that to me? I am called Pionius. Others said, O what great learning, and yet he stands thus. Pionius said, That learning you know rather by what you endured, famines and deaths and the other strokes. One man said to him, You too hungered along with us. Pionius said, I did, but with hope in God.

title: Imprisoned without burdening the faithful
english: When he had spoken these words, they were barely forced through the pressing crowd, packed so tight they could hardly breathe, and then they were cast into the prison and handed over to the jailers. Once inside, they found there a confined elder of the catholic church named Linus, and a woman named Macedonia from the village of Karina, and one man from the sect of the Phrygians named Eutychian.

While they were all together in the same place, the keepers of the prison learned that Pionius and those with him were refusing what the believers kept bringing. For Pionius kept saying, When we were in greater need we burdened no one, so how should we accept anything now?

title: Pionius weeping over the lapsed
english: And yet even in the prison many of the pagans kept coming to debate them and coax them away, and when they heard their answers they were amazed. And those Christian brothers who had been dragged in by compulsion also kept entering with loud wailing, as though in deep mourning every hour, above all for the devout and for those who had lived a good and orderly life, so that Pionius spoke the following words with tears.

I am punished with a new punishment, I am cut in pieces limb by limb as I watch the pearls of the church trampled underfoot by swine (Matthew 7:6), and the stars of heaven dragged down to the earth by the tail of the dragon (Revelation 12:4), the vine which the right hand of God planted ravaged by the boar from the forest (Psalm 79:14), and now all who pass along the way pluck her fruit. My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you (Galatians 4:19). My tender ones have gone by rugged roads. Now Susanna has been entrapped by the lawless elders (Susanna), now they uncover the tender and beautiful woman, that they may glut themselves with her beauty and bear false witness against her.

title: Famine of hearing and our own fault
english: As in the days of Esther, every city is shaken. Now there is no famine of bread and no thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord (Amos 8:11). Altogether the virgins grew drowsy and fell asleep (Matthew 25:5)? The saying of the Lord Jesus has come true: When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth (Luke 18:8)? For I hear that each man is handing over his neighbor, so that this may be fulfilled: Brother will hand brother over to death (Matthew 10:21).

Did Satan demand us, to sift us like wheat (Luke 22:31)? Fiery is the winnowing fork in the hand of the divine Word, to clean his threshing floor thoroughly (Matthew 3:12). Perhaps the salt has lost its savour and has been thrown outside and is trampled by men (Matthew 5:13). Yet let no one suppose, little children, that the Lord lost his power; we did. For he says, Is my hand unable to deliver, or has my ear grown heavy so that it cannot hear (Isaiah 59:1)? But your sins stand between me, God, and you (Isaiah 59:2). For we have done wrong, and some with contempt have even broken the law, biting one another and accusing one another, and we have been consumed by one another (Galatians 5:15). But our righteousness must overflow far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 5:20).

title: Refusing the Synagogue slander of Christ
english: I hear that the Jews are calling some of you also into their synagogues, so be watchful, lest an even greater and willful sin fasten upon you, and lest any of you commit the sin that cannot be taken away, the sin unto blasphemy of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31). Do not become with them rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah (Isaiah 1:10), whose hands are full of blood (Isaiah 1:15). We, for our part, neither murdered the prophets nor betrayed and crucified the Christ. Why should I speak many words to you? Remember what you have heard, and now carry through to the end what you have learned.

For you have heard this too, that the Jews say Christ was merely a man and died an untimely death. Let them tell us, then: of what man dead before his time has the whole world been filled with disciples? Of what man dead before his time did the disciples, and others after them, die so great a death for their own teacher's name? By the name of what man dead before his time, through so many years, have demons been cast out and are still cast out and shall be cast out, with all the other mighty works that come to pass in the catholic church? Yet they do not know that one dead before his time is the one who by his own deliberate choice carries himself out of life. They even say that Christ worked necromancy and by that art wrought a raising after the cross [verb lost — the charge being resurrection-sorcery]. What scripture, whether theirs or ours, says such things about Christ? What righteous man ever said it? Are not those who say it lawless men? How could anyone put trust in the words of the lawless rather than in the righteous?

title: Saul inquired; the lying spirit; received as children
english: I for my part have heard this lying fabrication, which they say has just now happened, from Jews repeating it ever since I was of a child's age.

For it stands written that Saul inquired through a ventriloquist-medium and said to the woman who practices divination in this way, Bring up for me Samuel the prophet (1 Samuel 28:8-11), and the woman saw an upright man coming up clothed in a double mantle, and Saul concluded that this was Samuel and asked him about what he wanted (1 Samuel 28:13-14).
What then?
Was the medium able to bring Samuel up, or not?
Those who say Yes have admitted that unrighteousness is stronger than righteousness, and they stand accursed.
But if they say she did not bring him up, then neither did she bring up Christ the Lord.
The exposure of this argument runs thus: how could the unrighteous medium, herself a demon, bring up the soul of the holy prophet resting in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22)?
For the lesser is commanded by the greater.
What then was it that Saul supposed had been brought up in that man's guise?

May it never be so, but the matter is something like this: angels of apostasy attach themselves to everyone who has become an apostate from God, and devilish attendants serve every sorcerer and magician and charmer and diviner.

And this is no marvel, for the apostle says, Satan himself refashions himself into an angel of light, so it is no great thing if his servants also refashion themselves as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14-15).
For how else will the Antichrist also appear as the Christ?
So she did not bring up Samuel; rather Tartarean demons, having made themselves like Samuel, manifested themselves to the medium and to apostate Saul.
Scripture itself will teach this, for the supposed Samuel who was seen says to Saul, And you today shall be with me (1 Samuel 28:19).
How can the idolater Saul be found with Samuel?
It is plain that he shall be with the lawless and with the demons that deceived him and mastered him.
Therefore it was not Samuel.

And if it is impossible to bring up the soul of the holy prophet, how is it possible for Jesus Christ in the heavens, whom the disciples saw being taken up and for refusal to deny whom they died, to be seen coming up out of the earth?
If you are unable to set these answers against them on your own, say to them, In this we are better than you who committed fornication and idolatry though under no compulsion.
And do not, out of despair, give your assent to them, brothers, but by repentance abide with Christ, for he is merciful to receive you again as children.

title: Euctemon sacrificed; the Ephesus lie; headlong
english: While he was still speaking these words and urging them to leave the prison, Polemon the keeper of the temple and Theophilus the commander of horse came upon them with their trackers and a great crowd, saying, See, Euctemon your leader has sacrificed; let yourselves be persuaded as well.
Lepidus and Euctemon are asking for you at the sanctuary of Nemesis.
Pionius said, Those who have been cast into prison ought to wait for the proconsul; why do you take his office upon yourselves?
So after many words they went away, and came back again with trackers and crowd, and Theophilus the commander said by a trick, The proconsul has sent orders for you to be taken to Ephesus.
Pionius said, Let the man who was sent come and take charge of us.
The commander said, But he is a princeps of rank; and if you refuse, I am a magistrate.
Then seizing him he drew his veil tight about his throat and handed him to a tracker, so that he nearly choked him.

So the rest came out into the marketplace, and Sabina with them, and while they cried with a loud voice, We are Christians, and cast themselves down upon the ground so as not to be borne off to the house of idols, the trackers lifted and bore Pionius head foremost, and since they could not get a grip on him, they kicked his sides with their knees and went crouching on their own hands and feet.

title: Refusal to sacrifice beside the altar
english: So they carried him in and set him on the ground beside the altar, where Euctemon stood by in idolatrous attendance.

And Lepidus said, “Why do you not sacrifice, Pionius?” Those with Pionius said, “Because we are Christians.” Lepidus said, “What god do you worship?” Pionius said, “Him who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.” Lepidus said, “Is it then the crucified one?” Pionius said, “Him whom God sent for the salvation of the world.” At this the rulers raised a loud shout and burst into laughter, and Lepidus cursed him.
But Pionius cried out, “Show reverence for godliness, give honor to justice, acknowledge that we share your mortal nature, keep to your own laws.
You punish us as men who will not obey, yet you yourselves disobey.
You were commanded to punish, not to compel.”

title: Rufinus rebuked and silenced
english: Then a bystander named Rufinus, who was counted among those supposed to excel in rhetoric, said to him, Stop it, Pionius, stop your vainglory.
But Pionius said back to him, Away with your rhetoric!
Away with your books!
Such things Socrates never suffered at the hands of Anytus — yet now everyone plays Anytus and Meletus.
Were Socrates and Aristides and Anaxarchus and the rest, then, vainglorious in your eyes, because they gave themselves to philosophy and justice and steadfast endurance?
When Rufinus heard this answer, he fell silent.

title: Garlands refused and return to prison
english: One man of worldly rank and glory, with Lepidus beside him, said, Do not shout, Pionius.
And he answered him, Do not force me; kindle the fire, and we go up ready.
Then a certain Terentius shouted from the crowd, Do you know that this man is also stirring up the rest not to sacrifice?
So they kept setting garlands upon them, but the prisoners kept tearing them off and casting them away.
And the public officer stood holding the idol-meat, yet he did not dare to come close to any of them, but ate it himself in front of them all.
And as they kept crying, We are Christians, and the authorities found nothing further to do with them, they sent them back again to prison, while the crowd mocked them and struck them with the hand.
And someone said to Sabina, Could you not have died in your own homeland?
And she said, What is my homeland?
I am the sister of Pionius.
And to Asclepiades, Terentius, who was then in charge of the beast-hunts, said, I shall demand you as a condemned man for my son's munificent gladiatorial show.
And Asclepiades said to him, You do not frighten me with that.
And so they were brought into the prison.
And as Pionius was going into the prison, one of his pursuers struck him a great blow upon the head, so that he wounded him, but Pionius remained silent.
And the hands and the sides of the man who struck him swelled with inflammation, so that the man could scarcely breathe.

And once inside, they glorified God that they had remained unharmed in the name of Christ, and that the enemy had gained no hold upon them, nor Euctemon the pretender, and they continued in psalms and prayers, strengthening themselves.

And it was reported afterward that Euctemon had demanded that we be forced, and that he himself carried his portion into the temple of Nemesis, and after eating some of it roasted he wished to carry the rest away for his whole household.

Thus he became a laughingstock because of his false oath, since with a garland upon him he had sworn by the fortune of the emperor and by the Nemeses that he was no Christian and that, like the rest, he would omit nothing belonging to denial.

title: Pionius questioned and condemned
english: After these things the proconsul came to Smyrna, and Pionius was brought forward and bore his witness, with the official record of the orders made, four days before the Ides of March.
Quintilianus the proconsul took his seat before the tribunal and asked, Who are you called?
He answered, Pionius.
The proconsul said, Will you sacrifice?
He replied, No.
The proconsul asked, What observance or sect do you hold?
He replied, That of the catholics.
He asked, Which catholics?
He replied, I am a presbyter of the catholic church.
The proconsul said, Are you their teacher?
He replied, Yes, I was teaching.
He asked, Were you a teacher of folly?
He answered, Of reverence for God.
He asked, Of what reverence for God?
He answered, That toward God the Father who made all things.
The proconsul said, Sacrifice.
He replied, No, for I must pray to God.
He said, We all revere the gods, and heaven, and the gods who are in heaven.
Why do you heed the air?
Sacrifice to it.
He replied, I do not heed the air, but the one who made the air and heaven and all things in them.
The proconsul said, Tell me, who made them?
He replied, It is not permitted to say.
The proconsul said, Surely it is god, that is Zeus, who is in heaven, for he is king of all the gods.
While Pionius kept silence and was hung up, he was asked, Will you sacrifice?
He answered, No.
When he was tortured again with the claws, he was told, Repent.
Why have you lost your senses?
He answered, I have not lost my senses, but I fear the living God.
The proconsul said, Many others have sacrificed, and they live and are sound of mind.
He answered, No, and the rest of the reply is lost.
The proconsul said, Now that you are questioned, reckon with yourself and repent.
He answered, No.
He was told, Why do you hasten to death?
He answered, Not to death, but to life.
Quintilianus the proconsul said, You do no great thing in hastening to death, for even men enrolled for the smallest sum despise death before the beasts, and you are one of them.
Since then you hasten to death, you shall be burned alive.
And from the tablet the sentence was read in Latin: We have ordered that Pionius, who has confessed himself to be a Christian, be burned alive.

title: The nailing and quiet death
english: They brought him in haste into the arena, for his faith was eager, and while the registrar stood by he stripped of his own will.

Then seeing how chaste and how wasted his own body had become, he was filled with great joy, and looking up to heaven and thanking God for keeping him so, he laid himself out on the timber and gave himself to the soldier for the nailing.

Once the nails were in him the executioner said again, “Repent, and your nails will be taken away.” He answered, “For I have perceived it,” though what he perceived is lost, and after thinking a little he said, “That is why I hasten, so that I may rise the sooner,” meaning the resurrection from the dead.
So they raised him upright on the timber, and afterwards they raised a certain elder Metrodorus of the Marcionist sect as well.
It so happened that Pionius was on the right and Metrodorus on the left, yet both faced east.
When the men had brought the fuel and piled the wood in a circle around them, Pionius closed his eyes, so that the crowd thought he had already died.
But he was praying in the hidden way, and when he reached the end of the prayer he looked up.

With the flame already rising, his face rejoicing, he spoke the final amen and said, “Lord, receive my soul” (Acts 7:59), and then, quietly and without pain, he breathed his last and gave his spirit as a trust into the keeping of the Father, who promised to guard every drop of blood and every soul unjustly condemned.

title: Pionius crowned in body after fire
english: Having completed such a life, the blessed Pionius, blameless and unimpeached and undefiled, with his mind ever bent upon God almighty and upon the mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Timothy 2:5), was counted worthy of such an end, and after winning the great contest he passed through the narrow door (Matthew 7:13) into the wide and great light.
His crown was made visible through his body as well, for after the fire was quenched we who were present saw him like the body of an athlete in his prime and in full adornment.
His ears had become reddened, and the hairs lay close upon the skin of his head, and his beard was adorned as with fresh down coming into bloom.
His face also shone, a marvelous grace again, so that the Christians were established still more firmly in faith, while the unbelievers drew back in terror with stricken conscience.

These things were done when Julius Proclus Quintilianus was proconsul of Asia, in the consulship of the emperor Messius Quintus Trajanus Decius Augustus for the second time and Vettius Gratus, four days before the Ides of March by Roman reckoning, by Asian reckoning on the nineteenth of the sixth month, on the Sabbath day, at the tenth hour, but by our reckoning while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom be glory unto the ages of ages, amen.
